title: Causal Multi-Task Demand Learning
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: Our information-design method tracks the oracle error floor and beats baselines, most clearly under strong confounding, as data per task grows.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots, confounding level by column, shared legend on top
description: A shared legend across the top lists five methods: DCMOML (purple circles), META (red squares), EB-GLS (orange triangles), DCUOML (green diamonds), and a black dashed Oracle (Bayes floor). Below it is a 2x3 grid of log-scale line plots. Columns are high, medium and low confounding. The top row shows intercept MSE and the bottom row shows slope MSE. The x-axis in every panel is K, observations per task, from 2 to 5. Every curve falls as K increases. Under high confounding, DCMOML sits just above the dashed oracle. META is clearly higher, and EB-GLS and DCUOML are an order of magnitude higher. Under medium and low confounding, META converges to DCMOML and the oracle, while EB-GLS and DCUOML stay far above. The eye goes first to the purple curve hugging the black dashed floor.
caption: Synthetic study: intercept (top) and slope (bottom) MSE against the number of observations per task, under high, medium and low confounding (log scale; mean over 10 seeds with 95% intervals, mostly smaller than the markers). The oracle is the Bayes floor for DCMOML's information set.
abstract: We study multi-task demand learning for retail pricing, where firms seek to estimate heterogeneous linear price-response functions across many decision contexts. Each context has rich covariates but limited price variation, motivating transfer across tasks. However, such transfer is complicated by endogeneity: prices may be arbitrarily correlated with unobserved task-level demand determinants. We propose a meta-learning framework that identifies the conditional mean of task-specific causal demand parameters despite this confounding, provided each task contains at least two distinct, locally exogenous price points. The key is to carefully design the information available to the learner. We condition on the full price history to address cross-task confounding, but withhold the demand outcomes associated with two locally exogenous price points to preserve identifiability. These withheld outcomes provide supervision through a randomized query. We establish that this information design is maximally uniformly valid for the squared-loss objective: any refinement of the conditioning set that reveals information about the withheld outcomes or the query index admits a data-generating process under which the objective no longer identifies the conditional mean causal target. Synthetic experiments demonstrate improved estimation of causal demand parameters under strong confounding, while retail experiments show improved held-out demand prediction relative to standard transfer-learning baselines.
